lessons.title: Nigeria's Economy: TNCs, Industry & Trade
lessons.description: How manufacturing, transnational corporations and changing trade links drive Nigerian growth.
lessons.content_html:
An Economy on the Move

Nigeria’s economy looks completely different to the one that gained independence in 1960. Then, around 70% of workers grew crops on small farms, oil had only just been discovered, and the country exported almost no manufactured goods. Today the share of agriculture has fallen to 22% of GDP, while services account for 53% and industry 25%. Behind that shift lie three forces studied in this lesson: manufacturing, transnational corporations and changing trade links.

Key Fact

Nigeria’s economy has shifted from mainly farming to a mixed economy. Agriculture is now around 22% of GDP, industry 25% and services 53%. Oil and gas alone provide over 80% of export earnings.

Changing Industrial Structure

Geographers describe an economy by its industrial structure. As Nigeria has developed, workers have moved out of farming and into manufacturing and services. Manufacturing is critical because it adds value: cocoa beans sold raw earn one price, chocolate bars made in Nigeria earn far more. Factories also create skilled jobs, train workers and pay taxes that fund infrastructure. The Nigerian government has set up Free Trade Zones at Lekki, Calabar and Lagos to attract factories with low taxes and reliable electricity. Major industries now include cement (Dangote Cement is one of Africa’s largest companies), food and drinks, textiles, vehicle assembly and growing pharmaceutical production.

Each new factory creates jobs directly — chefs, drivers, engineers, line workers — but also stimulates the local economy through the multiplier effect. A cement plant near Ibadan, for example, creates demand for transport firms, food sellers, mechanics and small shops. Tax revenue funds schools and hospitals. Skilled workers can move on to other industries, raising the country’s overall productivity. This is the engine of NEE growth.

Transnational Corporations (TNCs)

A transnational corporation (TNC) is a firm with operations in more than one country. Nigeria hosts dozens, including Shell, ExxonMobil, Chevron and TotalEnergies in oil; MTN (a South African TNC) in telecoms; Unilever in soaps and food; and Cadbury in confectionery. They are attracted by oil reserves, a vast consumer market and English as the language of business.

Advantages: TNCs bring foreign investment that the government cannot raise alone. Shell’s operations in the Niger Delta employ around 6,000 Nigerians directly and many more through contractors. TNCs train local engineers and managers, build schools and clinics under corporate social responsibility programmes, and pay taxes that fund the federal budget. Telecoms TNCs like MTN have brought mobile phones to over 200 million Nigerians, transforming banking and small business.

Disadvantages: Profits often leave Nigeria for the TNC’s home country. TNCs may impose poor working conditions or pay low wages. Worst is the environmental damage: Shell, Chevron and other oil companies have spilled millions of litres of crude oil into the Niger Delta over decades, killing fisheries. Tax avoidance through transfer pricing is common. Decisions about Nigerian jobs are often made in London, Houston or Johannesburg.

Changing Political and Trading Relationships

For most of the 20th century Nigeria’s biggest trading partners were the UK and other former colonial powers. That has changed. Today the largest single buyer of Nigerian crude oil is India. China has become the largest source of imports, providing machinery, vehicles and electronics, and is funding major infrastructure such as the Lagos–Ibadan railway through foreign direct investment. The European Union remains an important market for Nigerian agricultural products. Nigeria’s membership of AfCFTA from 2021 means tariffs are being removed on most goods traded between African countries.

Key Fact

Nigeria’s top trading partner for imports is China; its biggest oil customer is India. China has funded major projects like the Lagos–Ibadan railway. AfCFTA (since 2021) is opening up trade with the rest of Africa.

Putting the Pieces Together

Nigeria’s economy works because manufacturing, TNCs and trade are now reinforcing each other. Dangote Cement, a Nigerian-owned firm, has expanded across Africa using export earnings. International TNCs supply technology and capital. Free Trade Zones attract both. New trade links with China and India have replaced reliance on former colonial markets. The challenges — oil dependence, environmental damage in the Delta, regional inequality — are exactly what the next lesson on aid and quality of life looks at.

For 4-mark explain questions, structure your answer around clear cause-and-effect: TNC builds factory → creates 6,000 jobs → multiplier effect → growth. For 9-mark assessments on TNCs, weigh the advantages (jobs, investment, infrastructure) against disadvantages (oil spills, profits leaving, tax avoidance) and reach a clear judgement. Remember Nigeria’s changing trade links: China is now the biggest source of imports.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Nigeria’s industrial structure has shifted from agriculture (now ~22% of GDP) towards manufacturing and services; manufacturing adds value, creates jobs and triggers a multiplier effect.
  • TNCs like Shell, MTN and Unilever bring investment, jobs and technology, but profits often leave the country and oil firms have caused major pollution in the Niger Delta.
  • Trading partnerships have shifted from former colonial powers to China (largest source of imports), India (biggest oil buyer) and other African states through AfCFTA from 2021.

lessons.description: Types of aid, the environmental price of development and how it affects ordinary Nigerians.
lessons.content_html:
The Other Side of NEE Growth

The previous lesson focused on the engines of Nigeria’s growth — manufacturing, TNCs and trade. This lesson looks at the consequences. Aid has helped fund schools, healthcare and disaster recovery. But rapid economic development has come with a heavy environmental price tag, and the benefits have not reached every Nigerian equally. Quality of life has improved on average yet inequality remains stark.

Key Fact

Nigeria receives short-term and long-term aid, top-down (large infrastructure) and bottom-up (community-led) projects. Major donors include the UK, USA, the World Bank and Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.

Types of Aid Nigeria Receives

There are four main categories of aid. Short-term emergency aid follows disasters — the UN sent food and clean water after the 2022 Nigeria floods, which killed over 600 people and displaced 1.4 million. Long-term development aid funds infrastructure, health and education over many years; the UK’s former Department for International Development (DFID, now part of FCDO) has spent hundreds of millions of pounds on Nigerian schools and clinics. Top-down aid is large-scale projects organised by governments or international bodies — for example, the World Bank’s funding for the Lagos urban water network. Bottom-up aid is small, community-led projects organised by NGOs such as ActionAid Nigeria, which trains village women in farming techniques.

Positive impacts: Aid funds clinics that have helped cut under-5 mortality from over 200 per 1,000 in 1990 to around 110 today. Polio was officially eliminated in Nigeria in 2020 thanks to a combined World Health Organization, UNICEF and Gates Foundation vaccination drive. NGOs help women set up small businesses, raising rural incomes.

Negative impacts: Aid can be misused if government corruption diverts money from intended recipients — Transparency International has flagged this risk repeatedly. Aid can create dependency rather than self-reliance. Some critics argue donors attach conditions that benefit them, like requiring spending on companies from the donor country.

Environmental Impacts of Development

Nigeria’s rapid growth has caused serious environmental damage. The Niger Delta is the worst-affected area: oil spills from rusting pipelines have leaked over 13 million barrels of crude into the creeks and mangroves since the 1970s — equivalent to roughly 50 Exxon Valdez disasters. Spills kill fish and crops on which 60% of Delta residents rely for food. Gas flaring — burning off waste gas from oil wells — releases massive amounts of CO₂ and toxic particulates; Nigeria is one of the world’s biggest gas flarers despite official bans.

Beyond the Delta

In the north, growing populations and Sahel droughts are causing desertification — about 350,000 hectares of land turn to desert every year. In Lagos, fast urban growth has filled lagoons with waste, raised air pollution to dangerous levels and put pressure on freshwater. Industrial output has tripled since 2000, but environmental regulation has not kept pace, with factories often discharging untreated effluent into rivers. Climate change is a force multiplier: heavier rainstorms in the south worsen flooding while the north becomes drier.

Key Fact

Three big environmental costs: oil spills and gas flaring in the Niger Delta, desertification in the north (350,000 hectares lost a year) and air and water pollution in fast-growing cities like Lagos.

Effects on Quality of Life

For many Nigerians, life is genuinely improving. Average life expectancy has climbed from 47 in 1990 to around 55 today. Access to safe water has risen above 70% in cities. Mobile phone ownership is over 90%, opening up banking and education. School enrolment is rising. The economy has lifted tens of millions out of extreme poverty. Yet quality of life remains uneven.

Around 40% of Nigerians still live below the national poverty line. Inequality is sharp between regions: Lagos State has a poverty rate around 4%; Sokoto State in the north sees rates over 80%. Rural communities lack reliable power, with daily blackouts even in cities. The Niger Delta’s oil-bearing communities suffer poorly compensated pollution while wealth flows to Abuja and abroad. Boko Haram’s violence has destroyed schools and clinics in the north-east. Quality of life depends sharply on where in Nigeria you are born.

Putting It Together

Nigeria’s case study brings together everything in this unit on changing economic worlds. Manufacturing, TNCs and new trade links have lifted millions out of poverty and boosted Africa’s position globally. Aid has helped tackle disease and disaster. But the environmental price — oil pollution, desertification, urban smog — falls hardest on the poor, and the wealth created has not yet reached every region. The work of development is unfinished.

For 9-mark assessments on quality of life, weigh genuine improvements (life expectancy 47→55, polio eliminated 2020) against persistent inequality (40% poverty, Sokoto vs Lagos), and reach a clear judgement. Always link environmental damage to specific Nigerian places — Niger Delta oil spills, northern Sahel desertification — not generic ‘pollution’.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Nigeria receives short-term emergency aid, long-term development aid, top-down government projects and bottom-up NGO initiatives; aid has helped cut under-5 mortality and eliminate polio (2020).
  • Economic development has caused major environmental damage: 13 million barrels of oil spilled in the Niger Delta since the 1970s, gas flaring, 350,000 hectares of northern land lost to desertification each year, urban air pollution.
  • Quality of life has improved (life expectancy 47→55, school enrolment rising) but remains uneven — Lagos has 4% poverty while Sokoto State sees over 80%, and the Niger Delta’s oil communities bear pollution without sharing the wealth.

lessons.title: The UK Economy: Deindustrialisation & Globalisation
lessons.description: How traditional industry declined and a post-industrial UK economy emerged.
lessons.content_html:
A Different UK Economy

If you walked through Sheffield, Cardiff or Glasgow in 1970 you would have seen smoking chimneys, busy steelworks and miners coming off their shift. Walk those same streets today and you will find call centres, museums in old factories and university campuses where the pits used to be. The UK economy has been transformed by two linked processes: deindustrialisation and globalisation.

Key Fact

Deindustrialisation is the decline of traditional manufacturing industries — including coal, steel, shipbuilding and textiles — and the loss of the jobs they once provided. In 1970, manufacturing employed roughly 7 million people in the UK; today it employs around 2.5 million.

Why Did Traditional Industry Decline?

There is no single cause — deindustrialisation came from several pressures hitting at once. Cheaper foreign competition made UK steel, ships and textiles uncompetitive. South Korean shipyards and Chinese steelworks could produce the same goods at far lower wages. Outdated machinery in old British factories meant lower productivity than overseas rivals. Resource exhaustion mattered too: by the 1980s, easy-to-mine UK coal seams were running out and remaining coal cost more to extract than imported alternatives. Government policies in the 1980s, including the closure of unprofitable nationalised industries and reduced subsidies, sped up the loss of jobs in mining and steel.

UK coal output peaked at 292 million tonnes in 1913 and the industry employed over a million people. By 2015 the last deep coal mine at Kellingley closed and direct employment had fallen to a few thousand. Steel output has fallen from over 28 million tonnes a year in 1970 to under 7 million today, and shipyards on the Clyde and Tyne employ a fraction of their former workforce. The decline was concentrated in the north of England, south Wales, central Scotland and Northern Ireland — areas that built their towns around a single industry.

Globalisation: Goods, Services and People

Globalisation works in both directions. UK consumers now buy clothes stitched in Bangladesh, phones assembled in Vietnam and steel rolled in China — cheaper than UK-made equivalents. At the same time, UK firms sell financial services, education, pharmaceuticals and creative industries (film, music, advertising) to a global market. Container shipping, the internet and cheap air travel made this possible. So while globalisation took some industries away from Britain, it allowed others to expand worldwide.

A second feature of globalisation is the rise of transnational corporations (TNCs). Companies such as Tata Steel (Indian-owned, but running plants in Port Talbot) or Nissan (Japanese, but assembling cars in Sunderland) blur the line between ‘British’ and ‘foreign’ industry. Foreign investment now supports many UK manufacturing jobs that survived the decline.

From Industrial to Post-Industrial

As factory jobs fell, new sectors grew. Today over 80% of UK jobs are in the tertiary sector — services such as banking, retail, healthcare, education and tourism. The quaternary sector — research, biotechnology and digital industries — grew alongside it. London became one of the world’s leading financial centres; Cambridge and Oxford built clusters of biotech firms; the M4 corridor west of London hosts software and aerospace companies. The UK shifted from making things to designing, financing and servicing them.

Key Fact

The four sectors are: primary (raw materials — e.g. UK fishing), secondary (manufacturing — e.g. JCB diggers in Staffordshire), tertiary (services — e.g. London banking), quaternary (research and ICT — e.g. Cambridge biotech).

Government Policies that Shaped Change

Government decisions accelerated both the decline of old industries and the rise of new ones. The 1980s saw privatisation — selling nationalised industries such as British Steel, British Gas and British Telecom — which exposed them to market forces. Deregulation of the City of London (the ‘Big Bang’ of 1986) allowed financial firms to grow rapidly. Enterprise zones offered tax breaks to attract new business to former industrial areas like Tyneside and the London Docklands. More recently, regional growth funds and the Northern Powerhouse initiative aim to rebalance the economy by investing in cities like Manchester, Leeds and Liverpool.

For the workers and towns at the centre of decline, the change was painful. Mining villages in south Wales and Yorkshire lost their main employer, often with no comparable replacement. Unemployment in some pit towns reached 30% in the 1980s, and even today wages and life expectancy in former industrial areas trail the UK average. Newer service jobs were often based in London or the south-east, hundreds of miles from where old jobs were lost — widening the regional divide that the next lessons will explore.

A Connected Economy

Today, the UK is one of the most globalised economies in the world. London is a major financial hub linked to New York, Tokyo and Frankfurt; British universities export education to international students; UK car factories assemble vehicles using components sourced from across Europe and Asia. The transformation is not over — automation and the rise of remote work continue to reshape where and how people earn a living. Understanding deindustrialisation and globalisation is the foundation for the next three lessons on the UK’s post-industrial economy, regional inequality and global links.

For 6-mark ‘Suggest’ questions on effects, name specific places (Sheffield, south Wales, the Docklands) and quantify where you can — specific detail beats vague generalisations.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Deindustrialisation is the decline of UK manufacturing — coal, steel, shipbuilding and textiles — driven by foreign competition, outdated machinery, resource exhaustion and government policy.
  • Globalisation took manufacturing jobs abroad but allowed UK service industries (finance, education, creative industries) to sell worldwide and brought in foreign investment from TNCs.
  • The UK is now a post-industrial economy where over 80% of workers are in services, with quaternary research industries clustered in places like Cambridge and the M4 corridor.

lessons.title: Post-Industrial UK: Science Parks & Rural Change
lessons.description: Service industry growth, the green industrial example, and rural areas of growth and decline.
lessons.content_html:
After the Factories: A Service Economy

As traditional industries shrank, the UK economy did not collapse — it changed shape. The country became a post-industrial economy, where most jobs are in services and high-tech research rather than mining, smelting or shipbuilding. Three areas have grown especially fast: information technology, service industries and finance, and research clustered around science and business parks. Together they have created millions of new jobs — though they are not always located where the old jobs disappeared.

Key Fact

The UK’s post-industrial economy is built on three pillars: information and communication technology (ICT), financial and business services, and research clustered in science and business parks. Together they account for the majority of UK economic output today.

Information Technology

The ICT industry covers software design, mobile networks, cloud computing, gaming and digital media. The UK has more than 1.7 million ICT jobs and the sector contributes over £150 billion a year to the economy. Major hubs include the M4 corridor west of London (often called ‘Silicon Roundabout’s sibling’), Cambridge and Manchester. ICT is attractive because it requires only modest physical infrastructure compared with heavy industry — offices, fast broadband and skilled workers, rather than coal supplies and railway lines.

Service Industries and Finance

Banking, insurance, retail, healthcare, education and tourism dominate UK employment. London is one of the world’s top financial centres alongside New York and Tokyo — the City and Canary Wharf alone employ over half a million people in finance. The growth of universities has turned cities like Oxford, Edinburgh and Manchester into major exporters of higher education. The NHS is one of the world’s largest employers with over 1.4 million staff.

Science Parks and Business Parks

A science park is a planned cluster of research-led firms, often attached to a university. The Cambridge Science Park, founded by Trinity College in 1970, now hosts over 130 companies in biotechnology, pharmaceuticals and software. Co-locating businesses lets staff share ideas, recruits and equipment — what economists call ‘agglomeration’. Business parks are similar but for tertiary firms (offices, headquarters), usually on city outskirts with good motorway access.

Modern industry can be more environmentally sustainable than the factories of the 1970s. Nissan’s plant in Sunderland is the UK’s largest car factory and produces electric Leaf and Qashqai vehicles. The site is partly powered by an on-site wind farm of ten turbines, captures rainwater for use in production, and reuses solvent from paint shops. Newer manufacturing demonstrates that industry and environmental responsibility can coexist — an idea now spreading to steelworks (electric arc furnaces) and chemical plants (carbon capture).

Rural Areas of Population Growth

Economic change reshapes the countryside as well as the cities. Some rural areas are gaining population through counter-urbanisation. South Cambridgeshire is a good example. Its population has grown by over 20% since 2001 because:

  • Commuter access: the area is within 30 minutes of Cambridge and around an hour of London by train, so professionals can live rural while working in the city.
  • Quality of life: villages offer cheaper houses than central Cambridge, good schools, less traffic and more open space.
  • Remote work: faster broadband and the rise of home-working since 2020 mean fewer journeys are required at all.

The downsides include rising house prices that price out younger locals, traffic on small village roads and pressure on services such as doctors’ surgeries.

Rural Areas of Population Decline

Other rural areas are losing people. The Outer Hebrides off the north-west coast of Scotland have seen population fall by over 50% since 1900 — though the recent decline has slowed. Causes include:

  • Lack of jobs: the local economy depends on fishing, crofting (small-scale farming) and tourism — all seasonal or low-paid.
  • Out-migration of young people: teenagers leave for university and rarely return, leaving an ageing population.
  • Declining services: as population falls, schools, post offices and bus routes close, making the area less attractive still.

Local authorities in declining rural areas use several strategies. The Outer Hebrides council has invested in faster broadband to attract remote workers, supported small craft and food businesses through grants, and worked with the Scottish government to subsidise ferry routes that keep the islands connected. Affordable housing schemes try to keep young families on the islands rather than losing them to the mainland. Progress is slow, but population decline has flattened compared with earlier decades.

Key Fact

South Cambridgeshire (growth, near Cambridge) and the Outer Hebrides (decline, remote north-west Scotland) show how access to jobs, services and city links determines whether a rural area gains or loses people. Rural change is not one trend — it depends on location.

Why This Matters

The shift to a post-industrial economy is uneven. Some places — Cambridge, the M4 corridor, central London — have flourished. Others — remote uplands, former mining towns, isolated coastal communities — have not. The next lesson asks why this divide between north and south, and between thriving and struggling regions, is one of the biggest challenges facing the UK economy.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 6-mark ‘Suggest’ questions on rural change, contrast one growth area with one decline area — naming both (South Cambridgeshire vs the Outer Hebrides) carries marks. Use comparative connectives (‘whereas’, ‘in contrast’). For the ‘modern industry can be more environmentally sustainable’ question, your example must include specific green features — e.g. ‘Nissan Sunderland uses on-site wind turbines and recycles rainwater’ — not just a vague claim about being ‘eco-friendly’.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The post-industrial UK economy rests on ICT, financial and service industries, and research clustered in science parks like Cambridge.
  • Modern industry can be more sustainable: Nissan Sunderland uses on-site wind power and water recycling alongside producing electric vehicles.
  • Rural change is uneven — counter-urbanisation has grown places like South Cambridgeshire, while remote areas such as the Outer Hebrides have lost population through job shortages and out-migration.

lessons.title: The North-South Divide & the UK in the Wider World
lessons.description: Regional inequality, transport investment and the UK's links through trade and culture.
lessons.content_html:
A Country of Two Halves?

If you draw a line from the Severn Estuary to the Wash, you separate the UK into a richer south-east and a poorer north and west. Geographers call this the north–south divide. The pattern is not absolute — there are wealthy towns in the north (Harrogate, Cheshire) and pockets of poverty in the south (parts of east London, Plymouth) — but on most measures the gap is real.

Key Fact

Wages in London are around 30% higher than the UK average, while parts of the north-east sit roughly 15% below it. Life expectancy in Glasgow is around 73 for men, compared with 82 in parts of West Sussex — a gap of nine years.

Why the Divide Exists

The divide grew partly out of the previous lesson’s story. Deindustrialisation hit the north, the Midlands, south Wales and central Scotland hardest, because that is where coal, steel and shipbuilding were concentrated. The new growth sectors — finance, ICT, biotech — are clustered in London, Cambridge, Oxford and the M4 corridor. London also benefits from being the political and financial capital, attracting head offices, embassies and the highest-paid jobs. Connectivity makes it worse: a train from London to Brighton takes an hour, but Manchester to Leeds (less than half the distance) can take just as long.

The north–south description is a useful shortcut but hides smaller divides. Some London boroughs (Tower Hamlets, Newham) have child poverty rates above 40%, similar to deprived parts of Liverpool or Middlesbrough. Equally, the ‘Golden Triangle’ of Cambridge, Oxford and London is even richer than the rest of the south. The divide is partly a regional one, partly a city-versus-coalfield one, and partly a global-economy-versus-old-economy one.

Strategies to Resolve the Divide

UK governments have tried for decades to rebalance the economy. Some of the main strategies:

  • Northern Powerhouse: a strategy launched in 2014 to link Manchester, Leeds, Liverpool, Sheffield and Newcastle into a single ‘mega-city region’ with shared transport, science investment and devolved powers.
  • Devolution deals: giving city-region mayors (Greater Manchester, West Yorkshire, Liverpool City Region) control over local transport, housing and skills budgets.
  • Enterprise zones: areas with tax breaks for new businesses, designed to attract investment to former industrial sites such as Tees Valley.
  • Levelling Up Fund: a multi-billion-pound programme of grants for transport, regeneration and cultural projects in towns that have fallen behind.

Transport Investment

Transport projects are central to closing the divide because better connectivity attracts business. Major examples include:

  • Rail upgrades: the Elizabeth Line (Crossrail) opened in 2022 to speed up east–west journeys across London. The Trans-Pennine Route Upgrade is electrifying the Manchester–Leeds–York line. HS2 Phase 1 will eventually link London and Birmingham, though northern sections have been scaled back.
  • Roads: the A14 Cambridge to Huntingdon improvement (opened 2020) eased a major freight bottleneck. Smart-motorway upgrades have added capacity on parts of the M1, M6 and M62.
  • Airports and ports: Heathrow handles around 80 million passengers a year. Manchester is the third-busiest UK airport. Felixstowe handles roughly 40% of UK container traffic, linking the country to Asian and European supply chains.

The UK in the Wider World

The UK is one of the most connected countries on Earth. Its position straddling the Atlantic and Europe, English-speaking workforce and historic global links shape its economy and culture.

  • Trade: the UK exports around £700 billion of goods and services a year. The European Union remains its largest trading partner; the United States is the largest single-country market. Other big partners include China, Japan and India.
  • Culture: UK music, film, TV (BBC, Netflix UK productions) and football (the Premier League) are watched worldwide. The English language itself is a major export, with overseas students learning it bringing £30 billion+ a year into UK universities and language schools.
  • Transport links: Heathrow, the Channel Tunnel and the Port of Felixstowe make the UK a global gateway. Submarine cables across the Atlantic carry the majority of internet traffic between Europe and North America.
  • Political links: through the Commonwealth, the United Nations, NATO and trading agreements with the European Union, the UK shapes and is shaped by global decisions.
Key Fact

The UK’s global links run through trade (EU and US lead), culture (Premier League, BBC, English language teaching), transport (Heathrow, Felixstowe, the Channel Tunnel) and politics (Commonwealth, NATO, UN).

Even after leaving the European Union in 2020, the UK still does roughly half its trade with EU member states. Geography matters — the EU is the closest large market — and supply chains built up over forty years cannot easily be redirected. The Trade and Cooperation Agreement signed at the end of 2020 keeps tariff-free trade for most goods, though customs checks and paperwork have added cost and delay.

Why This Matters

Understanding the divide and the UK’s global links matters because both shape opportunities for ordinary people. A child born in Glasgow has different prospects from one born in Surrey, and a UK exporter relies on Heathrow, the Channel Tunnel and the Port of Felixstowe to reach customers. Closing the divide while staying globally competitive is the central challenge of UK economic policy — and a topic the next two lessons return to from the resource side.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 9-mark ‘Assess’ questions on strategies to reduce the north–south divide, weigh up several strategies (Northern Powerhouse, devolution, transport, levelling-up grants) rather than describing one. Use specific places: ‘Greater Manchester’ carries marks where ‘the north’ does not. For 4-mark ‘Explain’ on the UK’s wider links, link a specific example to a specific outcome — e.g. ‘Heathrow handles around 80 million passengers a year, supporting business travel and tourism that bring in billions in revenue.’
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The north–south divide is a real economic and social gap — wages, life expectancy and opportunities differ — rooted in deindustrialisation in the north and growth of finance and tech in the south-east.
  • UK strategies to narrow the gap include the Northern Powerhouse, devolution deals, enterprise zones, the Levelling Up Fund and major transport projects like HS2 and the Trans-Pennine Route Upgrade.
  • The UK’s global links span trade (EU and US dominant), culture (Premier League, BBC, English-language education), transport hubs (Heathrow, Felixstowe) and political networks (Commonwealth, NATO, UN).

lessons.title: Resource Management: Food, Water & Energy in the UK
lessons.description: Why food miles, water transfer and a changing energy mix are reshaping UK supply.
lessons.content_html:
Why Resources Matter

Food, water and energy are the three resources every country needs to keep working. Without enough of any one of them, businesses close, hospitals struggle and people go hungry. Geographers call the way societies plan, share and protect these essentials resource management. The UK has plentiful supplies of fresh water and a developed economy that can buy what it does not grow, but its supply systems are changing fast as imports rise, water demand shifts and the energy mix moves away from fossil fuels.

Key Fact

The UK now imports nearly half its food, transfers water from the wet north and west to the dry south-east, and has shifted its electricity generation from over 70% coal in 1990 to over 40% renewables today.

Food in the UK

In 1984 the UK produced around 78% of the food it consumed. Today that figure is closer to 60% — meaning over 40% is imported. Demand has changed: shoppers expect strawberries in December and avocados year-round. Add modern lifestyles that prefer ready meals, and the result is rising food miles — the distance food travels from farm to plate.

Year-round demand for ‘summer’ produce means UK supermarkets fly green beans from Kenya, mangetout from Peru and tomatoes from Spain. Each step adds to the carbon footprint, so movements such as ‘Buy British’, farmers’ markets and farm shops have grown in response. Many supermarkets now label produce with country-of-origin and carbon scores, and some chefs have built menus around seasonal British vegetables to push back against airfreighted imports.

Two further trends shape UK food supply:

  • Agribusiness: the rise of large-scale, highly mechanised farms producing cereals and dairy efficiently — but with concerns over biodiversity loss, fertiliser run-off and animal welfare.
  • Local sourcing: a movement toward shorter supply chains that supports rural economies and lowers food miles, though prices are usually higher.

Water in the UK

The UK has plenty of water overall — but it is not in the right places. Over half of UK rainfall falls on the north and west, while two-thirds of the population lives in the drier south and east. Areas of water deficit include London, the East Midlands and East Anglia, where less than 700 mm of rain falls a year. Areas of water surplus include western Scotland, the Lake District and Wales, with over 2,000 mm a year.

To match supply to demand, the UK relies on water transfer schemes. The Kielder Water reservoir in Northumberland (the largest in the UK) sends water south through the Tyne, while the Elan Valley in mid-Wales has supplied Birmingham since 1904. Demand keeps rising as population grows and people use more water at home (washing machines, dishwashers, gardens). Quality is also a challenge — agricultural run-off, sewage discharges and microplastics put pressure on water companies to clean water before it reaches taps and rivers.

Energy in the UK

The UK’s energy mix has changed dramatically. In 1990 coal generated over 70% of UK electricity; in 2024 less than 1%. The last coal-fired power station, Ratcliffe-on-Soar, closed in late 2024. Today the mix is roughly:

  • Renewables (over 40%): wind (especially North Sea offshore farms like Hornsea), solar, hydro and biomass.
  • Natural gas (around 30–35%): still the largest single source, used in ‘peaking’ power stations that fill gaps when wind drops.
  • Nuclear (around 12–15%): from stations such as Sizewell B and Hinkley Point B (the last reactor closed in 2022); Hinkley Point C is under construction.
  • Imports and other: via interconnectors with France, Norway and the Netherlands.
Key Fact

UK domestic supplies of coal, gas and oil are all in decline. North Sea oil and gas peaked around 1999 and now produces less than half its peak volume, leaving the UK increasingly reliant on imports and renewable generation.

Economic and Environmental Trade-offs

Every energy choice has both economic and environmental costs. Fossil-fuel extraction creates jobs and tax revenue but warms the climate; nuclear is low-carbon but produces radioactive waste and is expensive to build; wind farms are clean but face local opposition over views, bird strikes and turbine noise. Some areas with surviving North Sea oil and gas (Aberdeen) depend heavily on the industry for skilled jobs, while areas with new offshore wind (Hull, Grimsby) are emerging as a green industrial cluster. Resource policy is rarely just about engineering — it is also about employment, regional balance and climate commitments.

In 2019 the UK was the first major economy to commit by law to reach net-zero greenhouse-gas emissions by 2050. That target shapes resource policy across food (lower-carbon farming), water (energy used for treatment) and energy (rapid expansion of wind and solar). Interim targets include reaching net-zero electricity by around 2035. The pace of change here is faster than almost any other country — though the cost and the impact on workers in fossil-fuel industries remain contested.

Why This Matters

A high-income country can be food, water and energy insecure too. The UK’s rising food imports, growing water transfers and shifting energy mix all show how the modern resource challenge is no longer just about scarcity — it is about sustainability, climate change and security of supply. The next two lessons zoom out to the global picture and then close with one community renewable scheme that shows what sustainable energy can look like at small scale.

Examiners reward specific places, dates and figures over vague claims.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • UK food self-sufficiency has fallen from around 78% in 1984 to about 60% today, raising food miles and pushing back movements like local sourcing and seasonal eating.
  • UK water demand is concentrated in the dry south-east while supply is in the wet north and west, so transfers from Kielder Water and Elan Valley are essential.
  • The UK’s energy mix has shifted from over 70% coal in 1990 to over 40% renewables today, though imports and natural gas remain important and nuclear capacity is being rebuilt at Hinkley Point C.

lessons.title: Global Energy: Surplus, Deficit & Insecurity
lessons.description: Why energy demand is rising, what affects supply, and the consequences of energy insecurity.
lessons.content_html:
Energy: Why Demand Keeps Rising

Global energy use has roughly doubled since 1980 and shows no sign of stopping. Three main drivers explain why. Economic development raises living standards: as countries industrialise, factories, transport and air conditioning consume more power. Rising population simply means more people to feed, light and move — the world reached 8 billion in 2022 and is forecast to reach over 9.5 billion by 2050. Technology creates new demand: data centres for streaming and AI, electric vehicles and bigger fridges all consume more electricity than the equipment they replace.

Key Fact

Three drivers of rising global energy demand: economic development (industrialisation in China and India), population growth (world reached 8 billion in 2022), and technology (data centres, electric vehicles and air conditioning). Together they push demand upward by roughly 1–2% a year.

Where Energy Is — and Where It Is Used

Energy supply does not match demand. The wealthy regions of North America, Europe, the Gulf and East Asia consume the most energy per person, while sub-Saharan Africa and parts of South Asia use the least. Yet many of the largest reserves sit in countries that consume relatively little: roughly 50% of the world’s known oil reserves lie in the Middle East, while Russia, Qatar and the United States hold the largest natural gas reserves. This mismatch creates global trade in energy — oil tankers crossing the Indian Ocean, gas pipelines crossing Eurasia, electricity flowing across European interconnectors.

A typical American consumes around 75 megawatt-hours of energy a year — roughly ten times the figure for a typical Indian and a hundred times that of someone living in rural Ethiopia. As poorer regions develop, their per-person demand will rise sharply, even if total population growth slows. Climate-policy debates often centre on whether richer countries should reduce their high consumption while emerging economies catch up.

Surplus, Deficit and Energy Security

Geographers describe countries as having an energy surplus when they produce more than they use, or an energy deficit when they produce less. Saudi Arabia, Russia, Norway and Qatar are surplus countries that export oil and gas. Japan, the UK and Germany are deficit countries that depend on imports. Energy security is the goal: enough energy, reliably available, at a price an economy can afford.

Factors Affecting Energy Supply

Energy supply is shaped by several factors:

  • Physical: climate (sun for solar, wind speeds), geology (oil and gas formations, suitable rivers for hydro), and the existence of reserves (Saudi oil, Norwegian gas, Icelandic geothermal).
  • Cost of exploitation: oil from shallow Gulf wells is cheap to extract; deep-water Atlantic oil and Canadian tar sands cost two to three times as much per barrel.
  • Technology: hydraulic fracturing (‘fracking’) unlocked US shale gas; modern wind turbines have made offshore wind cheaper than gas in the UK.
  • Political factors: wars and sanctions (the 2022 invasion of Ukraine cut Russian gas to Europe), nationalisation of resources (Venezuela), or political alliances (the OPEC group of oil-exporting countries) can rapidly change supply.

Consequences of Energy Insecurity

When supply does not meet demand, the consequences ripple through whole economies and ecosystems. Five impacts are commonly listed:

  • Exploration of difficult areas: insecurity drives drilling into the Arctic, the deep Atlantic and tar sands — risky, expensive and damaging to fragile ecosystems.
  • Economic costs: when fuel is short, prices spike. UK gas prices in 2022 reached over five times their 2020 level, raising costs for households and factories alike.
  • Environmental costs: turning to alternatives like coal, lignite or burning wood imports raises air pollution and greenhouse-gas emissions.
  • Food production: modern farming depends on fertilisers, irrigation pumps and refrigeration. Energy shocks raise food prices — the 2022 spike pushed up bread, milk and meat costs across Europe.
  • Industrial output: factories close or cut hours when energy is rationed. UK steelworks, ceramics and chemical plants warned of closures during the 2022–23 gas crisis.

In some cases, severe insecurity drives conflict between countries over disputed pipelines, oil fields or electricity infrastructure.

Before 2022, Europe imported around 40% of its natural gas from Russia. After Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the EU committed to cutting Russian gas drastically, while sanctions and pipeline sabotage (Nord Stream) cut flow further. Wholesale gas prices in Europe rose more than fivefold in 2022, fuel poverty surged, and governments rushed to find alternative supplies (US LNG, Norwegian pipelines, Qatari gas) and to accelerate renewable-energy roll-out. The crisis showed how quickly energy security can be rewritten by political events.

Key Fact

Energy insecurity drives rising prices for households, slowing factories, falling food output, exploration in fragile regions like the Arctic and, in extreme cases, conflict between rival states.

Why This Matters

Global energy use sits at the heart of three of the biggest stories of the 21st century: climate change, geopolitical conflict, and the rise of electric and digital economies. Understanding why demand is rising, where supply sits and what insecurity does to people prepares you for the final lesson, which moves from the global picture to a single small-scale renewable scheme that shows what a low-carbon energy future can look like.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 6-mark ‘Suggest’ questions on impacts of energy insecurity, give specific examples (UK gas prices in 2022, drilling in the Arctic) rather than general claims. For 9-mark ‘Assess’ questions on factors affecting supply, weigh up at least two factors (physical vs political, or cost vs technology) and reach a clear judgement — markers reward a clear answer to the question, not just a balanced description.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Global energy demand is rising because of economic development, population growth and new technology — with the world reaching 8 billion people in 2022.
  • Supply is shaped by physical, cost, technology and political factors — the 2022 Russian gas crisis showed how quickly politics can disrupt supply.
  • Energy insecurity raises prices, harms food and industry, drives risky exploration and can fuel conflict — making the move toward sustainable supply urgent.

lessons.title: Sustainable Energy: Renewables & a Local LIC Scheme
lessons.description: Renewable and non-renewable sources and how a community micro-hydro scheme cuts poverty.
lessons.content_html:
Two Families of Energy

Almost every form of energy used today fits into one of two families. Renewable energy comes from sources that replenish naturally and quickly — sunlight, wind, flowing water, tides, geothermal heat and biomass. Non-renewable energy comes from sources that take millions of years to form and cannot be replaced on a human timescale — coal, oil, natural gas and the uranium used in nuclear plants. The world’s energy mix is gradually shifting from non-renewable to renewable sources, but the change is uneven and contested.

Key Fact

Seven main renewables — biomass, wind, hydro, tidal, geothermal, wave and solar — replenish naturally. Non-renewables include coal, oil and natural gas (fossil fuels) and uranium for nuclear power. Around 30% of world electricity now comes from renewables, up from under 20% in 2010.

Renewable Energy Sources

Each renewable source has its own strengths and weaknesses:

  • Wind: grows fastest where wind speeds are reliable. Turbines work well off coastlines (the UK’s North Sea farms) but face local opposition over views and noise.
  • Solar: photovoltaic panels generate electricity from sunlight. Costs fell over 80% in the last decade, making solar the cheapest new electricity in many countries. India and China lead in installed capacity.
  • Hydro: dams trap river water and release it through turbines. Reliable but disrupts ecosystems and can displace communities (e.g. China’s Three Gorges Dam).
  • Tidal and wave: exploit the rise and fall of the sea or breaking waves. Predictable but expensive to engineer.
  • Geothermal: taps underground heat. Iceland gets around 65% of its primary energy this way; the UK has very limited capacity.
  • Biomass: burning wood, crops or organic waste. Counted as renewable if regrown, but can compete with food production and produces local air pollution.

Non-Renewable Energy Sources

Fossil fuels still supply over half of global energy. Coal remains the leading source of electricity in China and India because it is cheap and abundant, despite the highest carbon emissions per unit. Oil dominates transport — petrol, diesel and aviation fuel — though electric vehicles are growing fast. Natural gas is the cleanest fossil fuel, used widely for heating and electricity. Nuclear from uranium produces low-carbon electricity but raises concerns over waste storage, accidents (Chernobyl 1986, Fukushima 2011) and the high cost of building new plants.

Oil, gas and coal stay popular for several reasons. They have very high energy density (a litre of diesel carries enormous power for its size), the infrastructure for extracting, refining and burning them is already built, and they are reliable on demand — unlike wind or solar, you can turn them on whenever you need power. Replacing them takes both time and trillions of dollars in new grids, batteries and electric transport. Even with rapid renewable growth, fossil fuels are likely to play a role for decades.

A Local Renewable Scheme: Chambamontera, Peru

For the AQA case study of a local renewable scheme in an LIC or NEE, this lesson uses the Chambamontera micro-hydro scheme in northern Peru, completed in 2010. Around 60 mountainous farming villages in this region had no grid electricity. Micro-hydro uses a stream’s natural fall to spin a small turbine. The scheme provides:

  • Power for around 60 households in a community with annual income of just £700–1,400 per family.
  • A 20-year lifespan with low running costs, making it affordable in the long term.
  • Local ownership and maintenance — villagers were trained by the NGO Practical Action to run and repair the system, building local skills.
  • Environmental sustainability — uses river flow, not stored water, so there is no large reservoir flooding farmland or displacing people.
Key Fact

Chambamontera (Peru) cost around £43,000 funded mainly by Practical Action and the Peruvian government. It pays for itself by lifting incomes — villagers can refrigerate produce, charge tools and study after dark, raising productivity and quality of life.

Why Chambamontera Reduces Poverty

Electricity is more than a convenience — it is a poverty trap broken. Before the scheme, families used candles and kerosene (expensive, polluting and a fire risk). Children could not study after dark. Coffee farmers had to sell beans wet and at low prices because they could not refrigerate or grind them locally. After the scheme:

  • Education improved as schools and homes had reliable lighting for evening study.
  • Health improved as kerosene fumes (a major cause of respiratory illness) disappeared from homes.
  • Income rose — farmers could process coffee on-site and sell at higher prices, reducing reliance on middlemen.
  • Skills grew as villagers learned to maintain the turbine, opening jobs in nearby valleys.

Big national grids are costly to build across mountains and isolated valleys. Small, local schemes — often called ‘intermediate technology’ or ‘appropriate technology’ — match the resources and needs of the community. They are cheaper, easier to repair locally and fit the geography. Schemes like Chambamontera show how renewable energy can leapfrog the fossil-fuel stage of development entirely, much as mobile phones leapfrogged landlines in many African countries.

Conclusion: A Sustainable Future

Across the last six lessons you have followed the UK from declining factories to a global service economy, looked at where food, water and energy come from, and seen the threat of insecurity at world scale. Chambamontera shows that the response can be local: a small turbine in a Peruvian valley brings electricity, jobs and dignity. The bigger picture — whether through North Sea wind farms, Indian solar parks, German heat pumps or Peruvian micro-hydro — is the same. Sustainable resource management is the central project of 21st-century geography.

For comparison-style questions, contrast renewables (low carbon, intermittent) with non-renewables (reliable, high emissions) using comparative connectives.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Renewable sources include wind, solar, hydro, tidal, wave, geothermal and biomass — all replenishing naturally and producing far less carbon than non-renewables.
  • Non-renewables (coal, oil, natural gas, uranium) still dominate global energy because of high density, existing infrastructure and on-demand reliability.
  • Chambamontera in Peru shows how a small micro-hydro scheme can lift around 60 households out of poverty by replacing kerosene, lighting homes and powering coffee processing.

lessons.title: Global Food Insecurity: Surplus, Deficit & Impacts
lessons.description: Why food demand is rising, what restricts supply, and the consequences of global food insecurity.
lessons.content_html:
A World Divided by Food

At any given moment, roughly 733 million people do not have enough to eat, yet in wealthy countries a third of all food produced is wasted. This contrast — plenty in some places, food insecurity in others — is one of geography's sharpest inequalities. Geographers map it in terms of surplus and deficit: regions where calorie supply exceeds what people need, and regions where it falls short. Understanding why the gap exists, and what it does to people and landscapes, is the first step toward fixing it.

Key Fact

Around 733 million people worldwide are chronically undernourished (FAO 2024, 2023 data). Sub-Saharan Africa has the highest regional rates of undernourishment — over 20% of the population in many countries. In contrast, North America, Europe and Australasia have dietary energy surpluses, averaging well above the recommended 2,100 kilocalories per person per day.

Global Patterns of Surplus and Deficit

The global pattern of food surplus broadly follows wealth. North America, Europe, Argentina, Brazil and Australasia all have average calorie supplies above 3,000 kcal per person per day — well above the recommended 2,100 kcal. Meanwhile, large parts of sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia and Central America experience food deficit, with averages below 2,000 kcal. The picture is not simply a rich-world versus poor-world divide: parts of South and South-East Asia have grown food-secure as economies developed, while pockets of food poverty remain in parts of southern Europe and the southern United States.

Two main drivers push global food consumption upward:

  • Rising population: the world passed 8 billion people in 2022 and is projected to exceed 9.5 billion by 2050. More people simply means more mouths, and most population growth is concentrated in already-deficit regions of Africa and South Asia.
  • Economic development: as countries grow wealthier, diets shift — people move from staple grains to meat, dairy and processed foods. Producing 1 kg of beef requires roughly 7 kg of grain and large volumes of water, so richer diets place far heavier demands on agricultural systems than subsistence diets do.

In China, meat consumption per person roughly doubled between 1990 and 2015 as hundreds of millions joined the middle class. This single dietary shift required a vast expansion of grain imports (for animal feed) and placed new pressure on global commodity markets. When China buys more soya, prices rise in Brazil's Cerrado, where forests are cleared to grow it. Diet change in one country can drive land-use change thousands of kilometres away — a vivid example of how the global food system is interconnected.

Factors Affecting Food Supply

Even where demand is growing, supply does not always keep pace. Six factors commonly limit food production:

  • Climate: temperature, rainfall and growing season length set the agricultural potential of any region. Drought in East Africa, flooding in Bangladesh or late frosts in the US Midwest can devastate harvests. Climate change is making extreme weather events more frequent, threatening production in the regions least able to cope.
  • Technology: high-income countries use GPS-guided tractors, precision irrigation, disease-resistant crop varieties and cold chains to maximise yields and cut losses. Many LICs lack access to these tools, so yields of staple crops like maize or sorghum can be five to ten times lower per hectare than in HICs growing the same crop.
  • Pests and disease: locusts stripped crops across East Africa in 2020–21, affecting over 23 million people. Plant diseases such as wheat rust and banana wilt, and livestock diseases such as foot-and-mouth, can destroy entire seasons of food production.
  • Water stress: agriculture uses around 70% of all freshwater withdrawn globally. In areas of water scarcity — the Middle East, northern India, the Sahel — farmers cannot irrigate crops, limiting what and how much they grow.
  • Conflict: wars disrupt farming, destroy infrastructure and displace people from their land. In Yemen, South Sudan and Syria, ongoing conflict has contributed directly to widespread famine. Farmers cannot plant or harvest when fighting is happening around them.
  • Poverty: even when food is physically available in a country, poor people may not be able to afford it. Poverty traps — inadequate land, no credit, inability to invest in seeds or tools — mean subsistence farmers stay on the edge of hunger even in relatively fertile areas.

Impacts of Food Insecurity

Food insecurity does not just mean hunger. Its consequences ripple across environments, economies and societies:

  • Famine: the most extreme outcome. Famine occurs when food insecurity becomes so severe that death rates rise significantly. The UN declared a famine in parts of South Sudan in 2017. Famines today are rarely caused by absolute food shortage — they are usually the result of conflict preventing access to food.
  • Undernutrition: chronic food deficits cause stunting in children, weakened immune systems and reduced cognitive development. Globally, around 149 million children under five are stunted. The economic cost is enormous — undernourished workers are less productive, perpetuating poverty cycles.
  • Soil erosion: when food is scarce, people over-farm land — removing trees for fuel, grazing livestock on fragile soils, tilling steep slopes. This degrades the land's future productivity, creating a downward spiral. The UN estimates that around 25 billion tonnes of fertile soil are lost each year to erosion, much of it in food-deficit regions.
  • Rising prices: global food prices spiked sharply in 2007–08 and again in 2010–11, driven by poor harvests, rising fuel costs and speculation. These price shocks hit the poorest populations hardest because they spend a higher share of income on food — in many African countries, over 50% of household income goes on food.
  • Social unrest: high food prices and shortage trigger protests and political instability. The 2010–11 Arab Spring was partly fuelled by rising bread prices. In 2022, food price shocks linked to the Ukraine conflict contributed to political crises in Sri Lanka and Pakistan.
Key Fact

Food insecurity causes famine, stunts the development of 149 million children under five, drives soil erosion that strips 25 billion tonnes of topsoil a year, triggers price spikes that hurt the poorest most, and contributes to political instability and social unrest.

Conflict causes food insecurity by disrupting farming and supply chains, but food insecurity also causes conflict by inflaming grievances over land, water and resources. This feedback loop is clearest in the Sahel region of Africa, where climate-driven drought has reduced pasture, pushing nomadic herders onto cropland and sparking violent clashes with farming communities. Breaking the cycle requires both peacebuilding and agricultural investment — neither alone is sufficient.

Why This Matters

Food insecurity is not an inevitable fact of geography — it is the outcome of decisions about investment, trade, conflict and climate policy. The next lesson explores the strategies being used to close the gap: from large-scale irrigation schemes to urban rooftop farms, and from biotechnology to the simple wisdom of eating seasonally and wasting less.

For 9-mark 'Assess' questions on food insecurity impacts, rank the impacts — famine is the most severe but affects fewer people than chronic undernutrition; soil erosion creates a long-term threat. Examiners reward specific facts (149 million stunted children, 25 billion tonnes of topsoil lost a year) over vague generalisations.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Global food surplus is concentrated in wealthy regions (North America, Europe, Australasia) while deficit is worst in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of South Asia, driven by rising population and shifting diets from grains to meat.
  • Food supply is limited by climate, technology gaps, pests and disease, water stress, conflict and poverty — often acting together in the most food-insecure countries.
  • Food insecurity causes famine, undernutrition in 149 million children, soil erosion, food price spikes and social unrest — making it both a humanitarian and a political crisis.

lessons.title: Increasing Food Supply: Strategies & Sustainable Futures
lessons.description: From irrigation to urban farming, and from a vast Pakistan scheme to a Kenyan sand dam.
lessons.content_html:
Closing the Gap: Strategies for More Food

Feeding a world of over 8 billion people — soon to be nearly 10 billion — means producing more food, wasting less of what we grow, and doing it without permanently damaging the land and water systems that agriculture depends on. Geographers group the responses into two broad camps: high-technology, large-scale interventions that can increase production rapidly, and sustainable, locally appropriate approaches that work with natural systems rather than against them. Both are needed, and both carry trade-offs.

Key Fact

Six key strategies to increase food supply: irrigation (expanding water access), aeroponics and hydroponics (soil-free growing), the New Green Revolution (biotechnology and GM crops), appropriate technology (low-cost tools for LIC farmers), organic farming (restoring soil health) and urban farming (growing food in cities). Each fits different contexts and income levels.

Strategies to Increase Food Supply

Irrigation brings water to farmland that would otherwise be too dry to cultivate. Around 40% of all food produced globally comes from irrigated land, which covers only 20% of the world's cropland. Modern drip-irrigation systems deliver water directly to plant roots, cutting water use by up to 50% compared with flood irrigation. Pakistan, Egypt and India depend on large-scale irrigation for their staple food supplies.

Aeroponics and hydroponics grow plants without soil — roots are misted with nutrient-rich water in aeroponics, or submerged in it in hydroponics. Both methods use up to 90% less water than conventional farming, produce higher yields per square metre and can be operated indoors year-round without weather risk. Their main limitation is high capital cost, making them most viable in wealthy urban contexts or where land is extremely scarce (such as Singapore).

The New Green Revolution applies biotechnology — including GM crops — to create varieties with higher yields, drought tolerance and pest resistance. Golden Rice, engineered to contain vitamin A, addresses deficiency affecting 250 million people. Critics raise concerns about corporate control of seed supplies, loss of traditional crop varieties and unknown ecological risks from gene transfer to wild plants.

Appropriate technology takes a different approach: simple, low-cost, locally maintainable tools matched to the resources available in LICs. Examples include the treadle pump (a foot-powered device that lifts groundwater for irrigation, costing around £25), improved grain storage sacks that cut post-harvest losses, and hand-operated seed drills that improve planting precision without heavy machinery.

The original Green Revolution of the 1960s and 1970s transformed wheat and rice yields across Asia through high-yield varieties, fertilisers and irrigation, averting predicted famines. But it relied on expensive inputs that poor smallholders could not always afford, favoured irrigated lowland farms over rain-fed uplands, and damaged soils and water tables through overuse of chemicals. The 'New' Green Revolution aims to deliver higher yields and stress tolerance through genetics rather than chemical inputs alone — though the ethical debates around who controls the technology remain unresolved.

Case Study: Indus Basin Irrigation Scheme, Pakistan

The Indus Basin Irrigation System (IBIS) in Pakistan is the largest contiguous irrigation network in the world. It draws water from the Indus River and its tributaries (the Jhelum and Chenab) through a system of three major dams (Tarbela, Mangla and Chashma), 19 barrages and over 58,000 km of canals to irrigate approximately 18 million hectares of farmland. Construction of the modern system began in earnest following the Indus Waters Treaty with India in 1960, which divided the rivers between the two countries.

Advantages of the IBIS:

  • Pakistan produces around 90% of its food from the irrigated Indus plain, making the scheme central to the country's food security for a population of over 220 million.
  • Major crops supported include wheat, cotton, sugarcane and rice — the scheme underpins Pakistan's agricultural export economy, with cotton textiles a significant export earner.
  • The system creates millions of agricultural jobs across Punjab and Sindh provinces, supporting rural livelihoods.

Disadvantages of the IBIS:

  • Waterlogging and salinity: over-irrigation has caused the water table to rise in many areas, leaving soils waterlogged and salt-encrusted. An estimated 6–10 million hectares of irrigated land is affected by waterlogging or salinity, cutting yields and in severe cases rendering land uncultivable.
  • Water theft and inequity: farmers at the tail ends of canals often receive insufficient water because those upstream divert more than their allocation. This creates sharp inequalities between head-reach and tail-reach farmers.
  • Glacial dependence: the Indus system relies partly on meltwater from Himalayan glaciers. As glaciers retreat under climate change, long-term water availability is threatened — an existential risk to a system Pakistan cannot afford to lose.
Key Fact

The Indus Basin Irrigation System covers 18 million hectares — the world's largest contiguous irrigation network. It sustains Pakistan's food security for 220 million people but has caused waterlogging and salinity on an estimated 6–10 million hectares, threatening future productivity.

Moving Towards Sustainable Food Futures

Large-scale production can feed more people, but if it degrades soils, depletes water and harms ecosystems, it merely borrows against the future. Sustainable approaches aim to meet current needs without compromising future food security:

  • Organic farming avoids synthetic fertilisers and pesticides, building soil health through compost and crop rotation. Organic soils hold more moisture and are more resistant to erosion, though yields per hectare are typically 20–25% lower than intensive equivalents.
  • Permaculture designs farm systems that mimic natural ecosystems — mixing trees, shrubs, crops and animals so that each element supports the others. It requires minimal external inputs and is particularly suited to smallholder farmers in tropical regions.
  • Urban farming uses rooftops, vertical gardens, allotments and community plots to produce food in cities, cutting food miles and improving access for low-income urban communities. Cities like Singapore, Detroit and Havana have developed significant urban food production.
  • Sustainable fish and meat means choosing certified sources — Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) for fish, RSPCA Assured or organic for meat — and reducing overall consumption, especially of beef and lamb which have the highest carbon and land footprints.
  • Seasonal food consumption matches purchases to what grows locally at the time, cutting the energy cost of heated greenhouses, refrigerated shipping and air freight. A locally grown tomato in July produces a fraction of the carbon of an air-freighted one in January.
  • Reducing waste and losses is the cheapest way to increase effective food supply. The UN estimates that around one third of all food produced globally is lost or wasted — reducing this by half would be equivalent to feeding an extra 1 billion people without growing any more.

Local LIC/NEE Scheme: Sand Dams and Food Security in Makueni, Kenya

In Makueni County, semi-arid Kenya, the NGO Excellent Development has built hundreds of sand dams since 2002. A sand dam is a low reinforced-concrete wall, typically 1–4 metres high, built across a seasonal sand river. As floodwater flows over, it deposits layers of coarse sand behind the dam. Water is stored within this sand — not as an open reservoir, so evaporation is minimal. By 2023, Excellent Development had supported the building of over 800 sand dams across rural Kenya (including Makueni County), serving more than 100,000 people in a region that previously suffered severe seasonal water and food shortages.

Each dam costs roughly £6,000–10,000 to build, using local materials and community labour. The stored water allows year-round irrigation of small vegetable plots — onions, kale, tomatoes — transforming what was a single rain-fed harvest into multiple harvests per year. Women in particular benefit: they no longer spend three to four hours a day walking to distant water sources, freeing time for farming, education and income-generating activities. Soil moisture around the dam also increases, improving the productivity of rain-fed land downstream.

Sand dams exemplify appropriate technology: they use simple materials (concrete, local rock and labour), require no electricity or pumps, can be maintained by the community without specialist engineers, last 50 years or more, and fit the landscape perfectly — seasonal sand rivers that were once obstacles become assets. The contrast with large-scale schemes like the IBIS could not be sharper: a sand dam empowers a single community at low cost, with no risk of waterlogging, salinity or displacement.

Conclusion

There is no single solution to global food insecurity. Large-scale irrigation like Pakistan's IBIS can transform national food security but brings long-term risks of soil degradation and climate vulnerability. Local schemes like Makueni's sand dams deliver immediate, sustainable benefits to communities most at risk — at a fraction of the cost. A food-secure future will require both approaches, alongside the cultural shifts of eating seasonally, wasting less and choosing sustainable sources.

lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Strategies to increase food supply range from irrigation and GM biotechnology to appropriate technology — each suits different income levels and contexts, with trade-offs between scale, cost and environmental risk.
  • The Indus Basin Irrigation System in Pakistan is the world's largest contiguous irrigation network (18 million hectares), sustaining 220 million people but causing waterlogging and salinity on an estimated 6–10 million hectares.
  • Sustainable approaches — organic farming, urban growing, seasonal eating and reducing the one-third of food that is currently wasted — and local appropriate-technology schemes like Makueni's sand dams offer long-term, low-impact solutions.

lessons.title: Global Water Insecurity: Surplus, Deficit & Impacts
lessons.description: Why water demand is rising, what affects availability, and the consequences of water insecurity.
lessons.content_html:
Water: The Resource You Cannot Live Without

Of all Earth's water, only around 3% is fresh, and two thirds of that is locked in glaciers and ice caps. The tiny remainder — less than 1% of all water — fills rivers, lakes and aquifers on which humanity depends. Yet that 1% is unevenly distributed, and as global demand rises, the mismatch between where water is and where people need it is growing into one of the defining crises of the 21st century. Geographers call this water insecurity — a state in which demand either exceeds supply or where pollution and poor infrastructure make water unreliable even where it exists.

Key Fact

Only around 3% of Earth's water is fresh, and less than 1% is accessible in rivers, lakes and shallow aquifers. Around 2 billion people currently live in countries experiencing high water stress, and the UN projects that by 2025 two thirds of the world's population could face water shortages.

Global Patterns of Water Surplus and Deficit

Water availability is measured as the volume of freshwater available per person per year, adjusted for seasonal variability. Water surplus regions — tropical Central Africa (Congo basin), equatorial South America (Amazon), much of South-East Asia and Scandinavia — receive heavy, reliable rainfall and have relatively small populations. Water scarcity is most severe in the Middle East and North Africa (Libya, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait), where rainfall averages below 100 mm a year, as well as parts of Central Asia, the Sahel and northern India where demand from rapidly growing populations outstrips supply.

Two main forces push global water demand upward:

  • Rising population: more people drink more, cook more and produce more wastewater. The global population passed 8 billion in 2022 and is growing fastest in already water-scarce regions of Africa and the Middle East.
  • Economic development: as countries industrialise and living standards rise, water use increases sharply. Industry (manufacturing, power generation) and commercial agriculture consume vast volumes. A single litre of bottled water requires several litres in production; a car requires around 400,000 litres to manufacture. Higher incomes also mean longer showers, washing machines and garden irrigation.

Agriculture accounts for roughly 70% of all freshwater withdrawals globally — most of it for irrigation. Industry takes around 20%, used for cooling power stations, processing food and manufacturing. Domestic use (drinking, cooking, sanitation, hygiene) accounts for only about 10%. This balance matters for policy: cutting domestic use has a modest impact; improving the efficiency of irrigated agriculture is the single biggest lever available for reducing global water demand.

Factors Affecting Water Availability

Several factors determine whether a country or region can access enough safe water:

  • Climate: rainfall, evaporation rates and seasonality set the natural water budget. Areas with monsoon climates receive most of their rainfall in a few intense months, creating seasonal extremes of flood and drought. Climate change is intensifying these extremes — wetter wet seasons, drier dry seasons, and shifting monsoon timings — making water planning harder.
  • Geology: permeable rock types such as limestone and chalk store water in underground layers called aquifers, which can supply water even in dry seasons. Impermeable basement rocks (much of sub-Saharan Africa) hold little groundwater, so surface rainfall is all that is available — and that is seasonal and unreliable.
  • Pollution of supply: industrial discharge, agricultural run-off (fertilisers and pesticides), untreated sewage and mining waste contaminate rivers, lakes and groundwater. In Bangladesh, naturally occurring arsenic in shallow tubewells poisoned millions of people who drilled for clean water. In China, rapid industrialisation has severely polluted many major rivers.
  • Over-abstraction: pumping groundwater faster than it recharges permanently lowers aquifer levels. In northern India the water table beneath the Punjab farmland is falling by around 1 metre a year as tube wells extract water for irrigation. Saudi Arabia has largely depleted its 'fossil' aquifers — ancient water that accumulated over thousands of years and will not refill in any human timescale.
  • Limited infrastructure: even where water exists, it cannot be used without treatment plants, pipe networks and pumping stations. Around 2.2 billion people lack access to safely managed drinking water, mostly because governments lack the money to build and maintain the necessary infrastructure — not because water is physically absent.
  • Poverty: poor households often pay more for water (from water trucks or vendors) than rich households do on tap, because they cannot afford the connection fees or live beyond the pipe network. In countries without municipal supply, collecting water from rivers or ponds takes hours each day, a burden that falls disproportionately on women and girls.

Impacts of Water Insecurity

When water supply is unreliable or inadequate, the consequences affect health, food, economy and politics:

  • Waterborne disease and water pollution: when people drink from contaminated sources, diseases such as cholera, typhoid, dysentery and diarrhoea spread rapidly. Diarrhoeal disease kills around 1.5 million people a year globally, including around 495,000 children under the age of nine, mostly in LICs. In 2010, an earthquake in Haiti damaged water infrastructure, triggering a cholera outbreak that killed nearly 10,000 people.
  • Reduced food production: agriculture needs reliable water to function. As aquifers fall and rivers run low, irrigated farmland goes out of production. In California's Central Valley, a decade of drought forced farmers to fallow millions of acres and draw down groundwater reserves. Across the Sahel, reduced river flow has shrunk irrigable land, pushing millions toward food insecurity.
  • Industrial output: factories, power stations and mines need water for cooling, processing and transport. In India during a 2019 water crisis, several cities reported that industries were shutting down because municipal water supply had failed. Thermal power stations, which need water for cooling, cut output when rivers run low during droughts.
  • Potential for conflict: where rivers cross national boundaries, upstream users who divert or dam water reduce supply for downstream countries. The Nile is shared by 11 countries; Ethiopia's Grand Renaissance Dam (completed in 2020) triggered a prolonged diplomatic and strategic crisis with Egypt and Sudan, who depend on the Nile for over 90% of their fresh water. The UN has identified over 150 potential future water conflict zones globally.
Key Fact

Water insecurity causes waterborne disease (diarrhoeal disease kills around 1.5 million people a year, including around 495,000 children), reduces food production (drought fallowing in California's Central Valley), cuts industrial output and power generation, and drives geopolitical conflict — most starkly over the Nile, shared by 11 countries.

Egypt receives virtually no rainfall and depends on the Nile for about 97% of its fresh water. Ethiopia, upstream, began filling the reservoir behind its Grand Renaissance Dam in 2020. Egypt and Sudan argued this would cut Nile flow during filling, damaging their agriculture. Ethiopia, one of Africa's poorest and most populous nations, argued it had the right to develop its own hydroelectric resource. No final legal agreement has been reached, illustrating how water scarcity can turn resource development in one country into an existential threat for another.

Why This Matters

Water insecurity is not an abstract environmental issue — it kills people, destroys harvests, closes factories and starts conflicts. As climate change alters rainfall patterns and as population and development drive demand ever higher, the gap between supply and need will widen in many parts of the world. The next lesson explores the strategies — from massive transfer projects to simple rainwater harvesting — that can close that gap sustainably.
